column4: The section’s famine-day meal appears as deliberate mercy: the righteous feed miskin, orphan, and captive while loving the food, so need is answered at a cost to the giver.
This continuation gives the meal’s inner source: they feed only seeking God’s face and neither repayment nor thanks, making the section’s mercy an enacted intention.
The next ayah says they fear a grim day from their Lord; that frames the section’s “day” as an event that shapes what one does for the hungry.
The feeding scene continues with God shielding them from that day’s evil and giving joy; it shows the outcome opposite to the hunger and fire that mark the section’s refused need.
This ayah’s hosts give the arriving emigrants preference over themselves even while in want, directly matching the section’s giving during scarcity and showing mercy reaching the hand.
Its account of righteousness joins giving wealth despite love to kin, orphans, the needy, and travelers with patience through poverty and hardship; famine-day feeding belongs to lived faith.
The section’s loved food in 76:8 has a close counterpart in the command that righteousness is not reached until one spends what one loves; it clarifies the cost within generous feeding.
On known days of provision from livestock, this ayah commands eating and feeding the distressed poor; it joins the section’s “day” and its specific act of feeding.
The sacrificial meat is explicitly for eating and feeding both the contented and the petitioner, extending the section’s response to hunger beyond one kind of poor recipient.
The next ayah says meat and blood do not reach God, but piety does; it makes the section’s inner mercy visible through the outward act of feeding.
The preceding surah rebukes people for not honoring the orphan, the opposite of the section’s care for the orphan whose good can be delayed or overlooked.
It also rebukes people for not urging one another to feed the miskin, directly reversing the section’s famine-day meal and its call to mutual compassion.
The denier of judgment is pictured as pushing the orphan away, a concrete reversal of the section’s act of moving toward an orphan in need.
The next ayah condemns failing to encourage food for the miskin, matching the section’s insistence that compassion becomes provision rather than feeling alone.
Those questioned in Hell say they did not feed the miskin; this gives refusal of the section’s central act as a stated cause of punishment.
This question opens the scene that 74:44 answers: its contribution is to place refusal to feed the poor inside the account of why people entered Saqar.
The condemned person is described as not urging food for the miskin, another direct reversal of the section’s feeding on a famine day.
The same punishment passage says there is no food except ghislin; against the section’s nourishing response to hunger, it depicts a meal that offers no care.
The deniers ask whether they should feed someone God could feed; this is the precise refusal the section counters by making the settled, provided city responsible to feed.
The garden owners plan that no miskin enter that day; their exclusion of the needy reverses the section’s opening of provision to the hungry.
The punishment passage says the people have no food but dari; it begins the same failed-meal scene that the next ayah says cannot nourish.
The fire’s food neither fattens nor relieves hunger, a stark boundary against the section’s food that actually answers hunger.
The condemned are sent to eat from the tree of Zaqqum, another punishment meal set against the section’s life-giving food for the hungry.
The next ayah says they fill their bellies from it; the image is consumption without the relief that the section’s act of feeding is meant to give.
They then drink boiling water over that meal, completing a failed provision scene in contrast with food or water offered to a needy person.
The drink is taken like thirsty camels, so this continuation keeps thirst present where the section’s broad root ط ع م includes even water as feeding.
The passage calls this their hospitality on the Day of Judgment; that reverses welcome to the poor visitor with a hostile “provision” on an event-day.
This ayah introduces Zaqqum as the provision of the sinners, a punitive counterpart to the section’s food given to vulnerable people.
The next scene says they eat from it and fill their bellies; it supplies consumption without the nourishing mercy of the section’s meal.
Their meal is followed by boiling drink, continuing the same failed provision scene through thirst.
The Zaqqum tree is identified as food for the sinner, an opposite kind of provision to the section’s food that sustains the hungry.
The next ayah says it boils in their bellies; this meal harms rather than relieves the hunger that the section directs people to answer.
Its continuation compares the boiling to scalding water, completing the passage’s reversal of nourishing food and drink.
Joseph’s interpretation names seven severe years that consume what people stored; it gives the section’s famine-day a prolonged agricultural setting rather than an ordinary date.
The preceding instruction stores most of the harvest through seven years, showing the preparation against scarcity whose later answer is feeding.
After the severe years, the next ayah promises rain and pressing produce; relief after famine sharpens what it means to feed during the hard event.
Joseph’s brothers arrive saying harm has touched them and their family, ask for full measure, and request charity; the scene gives concrete form to needy people coming to a provider.
Pharaoh’s people are seized by years of drought and reduced fruits, a direct famine setting that makes the section’s urgent feeding more than a one-day inconvenience.
They claim good fortune as their own but blame Moses for affliction; this adds a response to scarcity that contrasts with the section’s duty to answer another’s need.
Flood, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood follow as distinct signs; the crop-destroying scene makes food vulnerability concrete beside the section’s famine.
Sheba is shown as a settled town with two fruitful gardens and told to eat from its Lord’s provision and give thanks; this is a city already fed.
When its people turn away, the flood destroys that cultivated provision and leaves bitter, sparse growth; the reversal illuminates the section’s hunger-struck city.
The next ayah identifies that loss as recompense for ingratitude, completing the passage’s reversal from a provision-rich town to scarcity.
The trial explicitly includes hunger, loss of wealth, lives, and fruits, followed by good news for the patient; it joins the section’s famine and its call to patience.
The following ayah gives the patient’s words when calamity strikes, supplying a stance toward the event that the section pairs with mutual exhortation to patience.
The Lord of the House is said to have fed Quraysh from hunger and secured them from fear; the provision-receiving city becomes accountable in the section’s image.
The preceding command to worship the Lord of this House gives the response to the provision named in 106:4 and frames the city’s dependence.
A secure town whose provision came abundantly from every side becomes ungrateful and is made to taste the garment of hunger and fear, the section’s exact city-level reversal.
After that town’s hunger punishment, this ayah commands people to eat God’s good provision and give thanks, clarifying gratitude as the opposite response to scarcity.
Abraham asks that this city be secure and its inhabitants receive fruits; a provision-filled city gives the section’s hungry town a concrete counterpart.
Abraham describes settling his family in a barren valley by the Sacred House and asks for fruits for them; it pictures provision needed to sustain people where food does not grow.
The sanctuary is secure and fruits are brought to it as provision; this connects the section’s town to a place whose residents receive food despite the surrounding scarcity.
Rain comes after people have despaired and God spreads mercy; this joins the section’s drought and famine to relief arriving as an act of mercy.
Rain revives a dead land and is given as drink to many people and animals; it specifies why the section’s root ط ع م can include water and why drought threatens life.
The question about the water people drink makes the section’s dictionary claim concrete: nourishment can be drink as well as food.
The next ayah asks who sends that water down; it places drinkable provision in the provider’s hands alongside the section’s call to provide.
The passage warns that water could be made bitter, a specific reversal of the drinkable provision included in the section’s broad sense of feeding.
The harvest command says to give its due on harvest day and not waste; it links food production, a day of provision, and responsible distribution to the section’s famine meal.
The source-section root يوم is used for a day measured as a thousand years; this is a specific Qur’anic instance of one yawm carrying a duration far beyond an ordinary day.
Here a يوم is measured as a thousand years in the ordering of affairs; it echoes the section’s dictionary image of a severe day that carries days.
The ascent is assigned a يوم measured as fifty thousand years; it makes the section’s root يوم as event-duration tangible, though its scene is not famine.
In the fasting context, a person unable to fast may owe food for a miskin; this bridges self-imposed hunger to material provision for another.
An oath is expiated by feeding ten miskin from the average food of one’s household, making the section’s meal a measured duty from ordinary provision.
For one unable to free a slave or fast, the expiation requires feeding sixty miskin; it ties the section’s feeding to concrete provision at scale.
The charity allocations explicitly include fakir and miskin among other vulnerable recipients, locating the section’s response within a distribution of wealth.
The needy petitioner and the deprived are named as claimants in wealth, clarifying the section’s miskin as someone owed a share.
The preceding ayah establishes a known right in the wealthy person’s property; it explains the claim made for petitioner and deprived in 70:25.
The ayah says a right for the asker and deprived is held in believers’ wealth, matching the section’s view that provision reaches the needy.
It describes poor people unable to travel who do not press their requests and may be mistaken for self-sufficient; this sharpens the section’s concern for need that can be overlooked.
The ayah commends concealed charity given to the poor; it adds a way to answer the section’s need while protecting the recipient’s dignity.
Asked what to spend, the answer assigns good spending to parents, kin, orphans, miskin, and travelers; it closely matches the section’s vulnerable circle.
When relatives, orphans, and needy people are present at inheritance division, they are to receive provision and kind words; this gives concrete care to the section’s neglected groups.
The command to show good to kin, orphans, miskin, neighbors, and travelers broadens the section’s act of feeding into conduct toward people encountered nearby.
The distribution of gains explicitly assigns shares to orphans, miskin, and travelers, showing wealth directed beyond its holders.
The distribution from towns is meant to keep wealth from circulating only among the rich and includes orphans, miskin, and travelers; it illuminates the section’s duty of a fed city.
The passage describes people driven from homes and property who seek God’s favor; their displacement gives a concrete parallel to people forced toward another place by hardship.
The next ayah asks that rancor be removed from believers’ hearts and invokes God’s tenderness and mercy; it completes the emigrant-host scene with a communal disposition.
The command assigns the miskin and traveler their due and warns against waste; it distinguishes responsible giving from the section’s man who claims to have spent abundant wealth.
The next ayah condemns squanderers as kin to Satan; beside the section’s proud claim to have exhausted wealth, it marks waste apart from feeding.
If one must turn away from a needy person while awaiting provision, this ayah requires gracious speech; it preserves mercy when the hand cannot yet give.
The command assigns the miskin and traveler their due, calling it good for those seeking God’s face; it joins material aid to the section’s inward mercy.
The next ayah contrasts wealth increased by usury with zakat given seeking God’s face, clarifying which use of resources benefits others and endures.
The righteous spend in ease and hardship and restrain anger; this makes generosity through scarcity, as in the section’s famine day, a mark of character.
Abu Bakr is urged not to stop giving to a relative, needy person, and emigrant after being hurt, but to pardon; it joins mercy with renewed material care.
Asked about orphans, the answer says reforming their affairs is best and they are brothers; it makes practical care, rather than neglect, the measure of relation.
The command is to give orphans their property and not consume it; taking what should sustain them reverses the section’s feeding and delayed care.
Guardians must return an orphan’s property when maturity is reached and not consume it hastily; this answers the section’s image of good delayed or overlooked.
Those who unjustly consume orphan property are said to eat fire in their bellies, a direct inversion of giving food to the orphan.
The command protects an orphan’s property until maturity, continuing the section’s concern that a vulnerable child not be neglected before good reaches them.
The wall is repaired so two orphan boys can reach their hidden treasure at maturity; this portrays protection that lets delayed provision arrive.
The addressed person is reminded of being an orphan and sheltered; it grounds the following duty toward vulnerable children in remembered care.
The same reminder says he was found in need and enriched, connecting received provision to the section’s call to supply the needy.
The command not to oppress the orphan directly reverses the neglect the section traces to the orphan’s delayed or overlooked good.
The next command not to repel the asker matches the section’s poor visitors who come seeking people’s help.

The ayah calls the boat owners miskin and says they work at sea; it shows the precarious livelihood of poor people, while the source-section root س ك ن connects that status to provision needed to remain settled.

The source-section root س ك ن links provision to being able to settle; this ayah calls houses sakanan, so the bridge is that the miskin lacks the provision that lets a person remain housed, though this ayah itself describes homes as a gift.

After the rebuke for neglecting the orphan and not urging food for the miskin, this ayah describes inheritance being devoured without restraint; it shows wealth consumed in a way that withholds a dependent’s due.
The next ayah names intense love of wealth, locating the attachment behind the preceding neglect; it contrasts with the section’s food given despite the giver’s love for it.
The final ayah says they withhold ordinary aid; alongside pushing the orphan and not encouraging food, this makes practical refusal the opposite of the section’s mercy that reaches the hand.

Immediately before the statement that they did not urge feeding the poor, this ayah says they did not believe in God the Great; it reverses the section’s pairing of belief with mutual exhortation to mercy.
For a hunting violation during pilgrimage, the expiation may be food for miskin; it adds a specific duty to feed the needy from sacrificial provision beside the section’s hunger-day meal.

This ayah describes the servants of the Merciful as neither extravagant nor stingy in spending; against the section’s claim to have spent abundant wealth, it distinguishes measured provision from boasting about amount.
This ayah condemns those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God’s path; it gives a concrete opposite to directing wealth toward the hungry as the section requires.
The next ayah depicts that hoarded wealth as a punishment on the Day it is heated and used to mark them; it makes preserved wealth a failed answer to need.
Winds carry heavy clouds to dead land, rain brings forth fruit, and the scene ends by recalling resurrection; it gives a specific return of provision to the drought-struck land named in the section.
People rejoice when rain reaches them after having despaired before it; the ayah supplies the human turn from drought to relief behind the section’s famine-day urgency.
The next ayah asks the reader to see God’s mercy reviving earth after its death; it completes the rain scene as restoration of provision after scarcity.
Rain enters the earth as springs and brings out varied crops that later yellow and become debris; it makes the section’s drought and disappearing harvest a concrete cycle of provision.
Blessed rain brings out gardens and grain; this is a direct agricultural scene of the food whose absence makes the section’s famine day severe.
The next ayah calls the produce provision for servants and says dead land is revived by it; it completes the image of food returning to barren ground.
This command protects an orphan’s property until maturity and requires justice in measure and weight; it makes the section’s delayed or overlooked good a concrete duty of guardianship.
The covenant calls for good treatment of relatives, orphans, and needy people; it places the section’s specific feeding and orphan care within a direct command to treat these groups well.
The ayah rebukes withholding what is due to orphan girls and commands justice for orphans and weak children; it exposes a concrete form of the neglect the section counters.

Hypocrites ridicule believers who give generously and those who have only their effort to offer; this condemns contempt for contributions made under scarcity, beside the section’s care for the hungry.
Spending in God’s cause is likened to a grain that multiplies into abundant harvest; it contrasts wealth that seems spent with provision that bears fruit through giving.
The ayah says giving must not be followed by reminders or injury; it specifies how aid to the section’s vulnerable recipients can preserve their dignity.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by harm; it makes the section’s mercy a quality of treatment as well as food delivered.
This ayah warns that reminders, injury, and show can nullify charity; it marks the opposite of the section’s sincere, enacted compassion.
Those who spend seeking God’s approval are likened to a garden that yields abundantly with heavy rain and still yields with light rain; it pictures giving as fruitful even when provision is limited.
The command is to spend from good things earned and not choose inferior produce for giving; it sharpens what it means to feed the needy with real provision.
Satan threatens poverty while God promises forgiveness and bounty; this names the fear of scarcity that can block the section’s call to feed during a hard day.
The continuation says spending is for the giver’s own good and should seek God’s face; it clarifies the section’s account of mercy as aid given without making the needy repay it.
In a family-maintenance context, a person of restricted provision is told to spend from what God has given; it supplies a concrete measure for giving when hardship limits the means.

The ayah names Quraysh’s recurring seasonal journeys; beside the section’s fed city and 106:4, it adds the city’s regular movement and provision setting to the claim that its people were fed from hunger.
